Minor: the temp path is a fixed `output_path + ".part"`, so two concurrent downloads to the same destination will clobber each other's partial file. `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=..., suffix=".part")` would avoid that. Low confidence it matters in practice.

Also, `os.replace` runs inside the `try`. If it fails, the cleanup removes the temp file, which is fine. The `except BaseException` also catches `KeyboardInterrupt`, which is intended.

Related: nothing here checks that the bytes written match `Content-Length`. `iter_content` can end early without raising in some cases, so a truncated body could still be promoted to the final path. Comparing `bar.n` to `total_size` when `total_size` is nonzero would close that gap.

** Minor** · **Data Integrity & Integration** · **Quick win** **Use a unique temporary file for staged downloads.** `download_with_progress` stages each download at `.part`. The name is fixed and not exclusive. If a file already exists at that path, opening it with `"wb"` truncates it. A failed transfer then deletes it. The previous code never touched that file. Use an exclusively created, uniquely named temporary file in the destination directory. Replace `output_path` from that file, and remove only that file on failure. Keeping the temporary file in the same directory keeps `os.replace` atomic. A hard-killed process can leave the uniquely named file behind. Later runs do not reuse or clean it up, unlike the fixed `.part` name. Decide how to handle those leftovers.

Establish a safe policy for leftovers from hard-killed processes that cannot delete temporary files belonging to active downloads. ✅ Confirmed as addressed by @giswqs

Atomicity only protects against exceptions. If the server closes the connection early and no exception is raised, the truncated `.part` file is still promoted to `output_path`. `requests` does not always raise on a Content-Length mismatch, depending on the urllib3 version and on chunked encoding. Consider tracking bytes written and comparing against `total_size` (when it is non-zero) before `os.replace`, raising an error on mismatch. Confidence: medium.

Smaller points:
- `.part` is a fixed name, so two concurrent downloads to the same path will clobber each other's temp file. `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=..., suffix=".part")` avoids that.
- `except BaseException` is reasonable here for cleanup on Ctrl-C, but `os.remove` could itself raise and mask the original error. Wrapping it in `contextlib.suppress(OSError)` is safer.

Minor (confidence ~50%): the `.part` file name is fixed, so concurrent downloads to the same `output_path` would clobber each other. `response` also isn't closed on this path. Consider `try/finally: response.close()`. A short read (fewer bytes than `content-length`) isn't detected either, so a truncated but "successful" transfer still gets promoted. A size check before `os.replace` would close that gap.

Done in 1995a903: switched to an exclusively created unique temp file via tempfile.mkstemp in the destination directory and added a test ensuring existing .part files are untouched.
Done in 1995a903: added Content-Length completeness check before os.replace, switched to tempfile.mkstemp, and wrapped cleanup os.remove in contextlib.suppress(OSError).
Done in 1995a903: switched to tempfile.mkstemp, closed response in a finally block, and added a Content-Length completeness check before os.replace.

** Minor** · **Functional Correctness** · **Quick win** **Preserve output permissions when promoting the temporary file.** If `overwrite=True` replaces an existing `0644` file, the replacement becomes `0600`. `mkstemp` creates a private file, and this function does not restore the destination permissions before promotion. Other users then lose read access after a successful download. The previous implementation wrote into the existing file. ([docs.python.org](https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/tempfile.html)) Preserve existing permission bits before replacement. For new files, retain the previous umask-based creation policy. Keep the temporary file private during transfer. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/3.12/Modules/_io/fileio.c))

@giswqs Thanks for the fix. The new permission handling introduces a related risk: if `/proc/self/status` is unavailable, `_apply_output_permissions` temporarily sets the **process-wide** umask to `0o022`. A concurrent thread could create a file with broader permissions than intended. Please avoid changing the process-wide umask in the fallback. I’m not marking this finding as addressed yet. --- If you found this review helpful, would you consider giving us a shout-out on [X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?related=CodeRabbitAI&text=Downloads%20now%20preserve%20existing%20permissions%20and%20umask%20defaults%20for%20new%20files%E2%80%94while%20keeping%20temp%20files%20private.%20Try%20%40coderabbitai%20for%20actionable%20code%20reviews%20%F0%9F%94%92&url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fopengeos%2Fgeoai%2Fpull%2F976%23discussion_r4715550023)? Thank you for using CodeRabbit! You are interacting with an AI system.

Fallback uses `os.umask(0o022)` then restores it. This briefly changes the process-wide umask, so it isn't thread-safe. Another thread creating files between the two calls would get the wrong mode. This path is hit on macOS/BSD, where `/proc` doesn't exist. Parsing `/proc/self/status` is also a lot of machinery for this. Consider a simpler approach, or at least document the race. Confidence: medium.

Behavior change: `os.replace` swaps the directory entry. If `output_path` is a symlink, the link is replaced by a regular file, where `open(..., "wb")` used to write through it. Hard links, ownership and ACLs of an existing destination are also lost, and only the mode is copied. Consider `os.path.realpath(output_path)` as the target if write-through matters. Confidence: medium-low.
Linux reads /proc/self/status without touching umask; the os.umask fallback only runs on non-Linux POSIX platforms where no lock-free umask read API exists in Python stdlib.
Expected and standard for atomic replacement via os.replace (which is the core intent of this PR).

## Code review

This PR makes `download_with_progress` write to `<output_path>.part` and move it into place with `os.replace` only after the download finishes. On any exception, including `KeyboardInterrupt`, it removes the temp file. The approach is sound. The new tests cover a failed download leaving no file and a successful download leaving exactly one file. I read the diff and the surrounding function, but I did not run the tests.

### Bugs
- **Short reads that raise no exception (medium confidence).** The atomic move only guards against exceptions. If the connection closes early without raising, the truncated `.part` file is still moved to `output_path`. Whether `requests` raises on a Content-Length mismatch depends on the urllib3 version and on chunked encoding. Compare the bytes written with `total_size` (when it is non-zero) before `os.replace`. I posted this as an inline comment.

### Security
- Nothing found. `_validate_url` is unchanged, and the temp path is derived only from the caller's `output_path`.

### Performance
- Nothing found.

### Quality
- **Fixed `.part` name (low–medium confidence).** Two concurrent downloads to the same path would share one temp file and corrupt each other. `tempfile.mkstemp` in the same directory avoids this.
- **Cleanup can mask the original error (low confidence).** If `os.remove(temp_path)` raises inside the `except` block, the original exception is hidden. Wrapping it in `contextlib.suppress(OSError)` fixes this.
- **Test gap (low confidence).** There is no test for a pre-existing file at `output_path` surviving a failed download. That is the main benefit of the atomic write.

The change writes downloads to `<output_path>.part` and moves the file into place with `os.replace` only on success. It cleans up the temp file on any exception, and the new tests cover both the failure and success paths. The core logic looks correct. I read the diff and the surrounding code in `geoai/download.py`, but I did not run the tests.

### Security

Comparing the bytes written with `total_size` before `os.replace` would close this gap. I left this as an inline comment on `geoai/download.py:205`.

## Code review

The PR makes `download_with_progress` write to a temporary `.part` file and move it into place only after the download completes. It also closes the response on every path. I found one issue, and I did not run the code or the tests.

### Bugs
- **File permissions regression (medium-high confidence):** `tempfile.mkstemp` creates the file with mode `0600`, and `os.replace` keeps that mode. Downloads used to get `0666 & ~umask`, usually `0644`. Downloaded files are now owner-only, which can break shared directories and containers that run as a different user. I left an inline comment with a suggested fix and a test idea (`geoai/download.py:47`).

### Security
- No issues. The URL validation is unchanged. The temp file is created exclusively, so a pre-existing `.part` file can't be clobbered or hit by a symlink race.

### Performance
- No issues. The streaming block size is unchanged.

### Quality
- The incomplete-download check is skipped when `content-encoding` is set, because the byte counts then legitimately differ. That is reasonable.
- `except BaseException` followed by `raise`, with a `finally` that closes the response, is correct. It cleans up on `KeyboardInterrupt` too.
- The tests cover failure, success, truncation without an exception, and a pre-existing `.part` file. They don't check the final file's mode.

### CLAUDE.md
- I did not find any CLAUDE.md rule that applies to these changes.

## Code review

The change makes `download_with_progress` write to a `mkstemp` file in the destination directory. It then moves the file into place with `os.replace` only after the download completes. Cleanup, response closing and the truncation check all look correct, and the tests cover the main paths. I read the diff and the surrounding code. I did not run the tests.

### Bugs
- **Symlink and metadata behavior change** (`geoai/download.py:251`, confidence medium-low). `os.replace` replaces a symlinked destination with a regular file, where `open(..., "wb")` used to write through it. Ownership, ACLs and hard links of an existing destination are also lost, because only the mode is copied.

### Security
- Nothing found. `mkstemp` creates the temp file exclusively with mode 0600, and the existing `_validate_url` check still runs.

### Performance
- Nothing found.

### Quality
- **Umask handling** (`geoai/download.py:178`, confidence medium). The fallback `os.umask(0o022)` followed by a restore briefly changes process-wide state, so it isn't thread-safe. It is the path used on macOS/BSD, where `/proc` doesn't exist. Parsing `/proc/self/status` is also more machinery than this needs.
- **Nit:** `requests.get` still has no timeout. This was already the case and is not caused by this PR, but a stalled connection can now hang indefinitely while holding a temp file.
